1	# Instructions for *ACL Proceedings
2	
3	The following instructions are for authors of papers submitted for review to ACL conferences (hereafter, "review version") or paper accepted for publication in its proceedings (hereafter, "final version").
4	All authors are required to adhere to these specifications.
5	
6	## Style Files
7	
8	*ACL provides style files for LaTeX and Microsoft Word that meet these requirements. They can be found at:
9	
10	> https://acl-org.github.io/ACLPUB/
11	
12	We strongly recommend the use of these style files, which have been appropriately tailored for the *ACL proceedings.
13	
14	## Paper Length
15	
16	The conference accepts submissions of long papers and short papers.
17	Review versions of long papers may have up to eight (8) pages of content plus unlimited pages for references.
18	Upon acceptance, final versions of long papers will be given one additional page -- up to nine (9) pages of content plus unlimited pages for acknowledgements and references -- so that reviewers' comments can be taken into account.
19	Review versions of short papers may have up to four (4) pages of content, plus unlimited pages for references.
20	Final versions of short papers may have up to five (5) pages, plus unlimited pages for acknowledgements and references.
21	For both long and short papers, all figures and tables that are part of the main text must fit within these page limits.
22	
23	The conference encourages submission of appendices and supplementary material, which are not required to fit within these page limits. However, review versions of papers must be self-contained: it is optional for reviewers to look at appendices or supplementary material. Please see [Appendices](#Appendices) and [Supplementary](#Supplementary Material) for more information.
24	
25	Review versions should not refer, for further detail, to documents, code or data resources that are not available to the reviewers.
26	
27	Papers that do not conform to these requirements may be rejected without review.
28	
29	Workshop chairs may have different rules for allowed length and whether appendices or supplementary materials are welcome.
30	As always, the respective call for papers is the authoritative source.
31	
32	## Anonymity
33	
34	As reviewing will be double-blind, review versions must not include any identifying information about the authors (such as names, affiliations, or URLs).
35	Self-references that reveal the author's identity, e.g.,
36	
37	> We previously showed (Gusfield, 1997)...
38	
39	must be avoided, and anonymous citations, e.g.,
40	
41	> We previously showed (Anonymous, 1997)...
42	
43	should also be avoided. Instead, use citations such as
44	
45	> Gusfield (1997) previously showed...
46	
47	Review versions must not include acknowledgements.
48	
49	**Papers that do not conform to these requirements may be rejected without review.**
50	
51	Any preliminary non-archival versions of submitted papers should be listed in the submission form but not in the review version of the paper.
52	Reviewers are generally aware that authors may present preliminary versions of their work in other venues, but will not be provided the list of previous presentations from the submission form.
53	
54	Once a paper has been accepted to the conference, the final version should include the author's names and affiliations, and is allowed to use self-references.
55	
56	## Multiple Submission
57	
58	Papers that have been or will be submitted to other meetings or publications must indicate this at submission time in the START submission form, and must be withdrawn from the other venues if accepted by *ACL.
59	Authors of papers accepted for presentation at *ACL must notify the program chairs by the deadline for final versions ("camera-ready deadline") whether the paper will be presented.
60	We will not accept for publication or presentation any papers that overlap significantly in content or results with papers that will be (or have been) published elsewhere.
61	
62	Authors submitting more than one paper to *ACL must ensure that submissions do not overlap significantly (>25%) with each other in content or results.
63	
64	## Formatting Instructions
65	
66	### File Format
67	
68	Papers must be in Adobe Portable Document Format (PDF).
69	Please make sure that your PDF file embeds all necessary fonts (especially for tree diagrams, symbols, and Asian languages).
70	When you print or create the PDF file, there is usually an option in your printer setup to include none, all or just non-standard fonts.
71	Please make sure that you select the option of including *all* the fonts.
72	**Before sending it, test your PDF by printing it from a computer different from the one where it was created.**
73	
74	Some word processors may generate very large PDF files, where each page is rendered as an image.
75	Such images may reproduce poorly.
76	In this case, try alternative ways to obtain the PDF.
77	
78	All papers must use **A4 paper format** (21 cm x 29.7 cm).
79	Papers must not be submitted with any other paper size.
80	
81	If you cannot meet the above requirements, please contact the publication chairs as soon as possible.
82	
83	### Layout
84	
85	All text except for page numbers must fit within the margins.
86	
87	Review versions should have page numbers, centered in the bottom margin, but **pages should not be numbered in the final version.**
88	
89	Manuscripts must be set in two columns.
90	Exceptions to the two-column format include the title, authors' names and complete addresses, which must be centered at the top of the first page, and any full-width figures or tables.
91	
92	The exact dimensions for a page on A4 paper are:
93	
94	* Left margin: 2.5 cm
95	* Right margin: 2.5 cm
96	* Top margin: 2.5 cm
97	* Bottom margin: 2.5 cm
98	* Column width: 7.7 cm
99	* Column height: 24.7 cm
100	* Gap between columns: 0.6 cm
101	
102	In the review version, a ruler (line numbers in the left and right margins of the article) should be printed, so that reviewers may comment on particular lines in the paper.
103	The ruler should not change the appearance of any other content on the page.
104	The final version should not contain a ruler.
105	
106	### Fonts
107	
108	All text (except non-Latin scripts and mathematical formulas) should be set in **Times Roman**.
109	If Times Roman is unavailable, you may use **Times New Roman** or **Computer Modern Roman.**
110	
111	The following table specifies what font sizes and styles must be used for each type of text in the manuscript.
112	
113	| Type of Text          | Font Size | Style |
114	| --------------------- | --------- | ----- |
115	| paper title           | 15 pt     | bold  |
116	| author names          | 12 pt     | bold  |
117	| author affiliation    | 12 pt     |       |
118	| the word ``Abstract'' | 12 pt     | bold  |
119	| section titles        | 12 pt     | bold  |
120	| subsection titles     | 11 pt     | bold  |
121	| document text         | 11 pt     |       |
122	| captions              | 10 pt     |       |
123	| abstract text         | 10 pt     |       |
124	| bibliography          | 10 pt     |       |
125	| footnotes             | 9 pt      |       |
126	
127	### Title and Authors
128	
129	Center the title, author's name(s) and affiliation(s) across both columns.
130	
131	Place the title centered at the top of the first page, in 15-point bold.
132	Long titles should be typed on two lines without a blank line intervening.
133	Put the title 2.5 cm from the top of the page.
134	Write the title in [title case](https://apastyle.apa.org/style-grammar-guidelines/capitalization/title-case); do not write the title in all capital letters, except for acronyms (e.g., "BLEU") or proper nouns ("English") that are normally uppercased or capitalized.
135	
136	Place the author name(s) and affiliation(s) under the title.
137	Write authors' full names; do not abbreviate given names to initials, unless they are normally written as initials ("Margaret Mitchell", not "M. Mitchell").
138	Do not format surnames in all capitals ("Mitchell", not "MITCHELL").
139	
140	Do not use footnotes for affiliations.
141	The affiliation should contain the author's complete address, and if possible, an electronic mail address.
142	
143	The title, author names and addresses should be completely identical to those entered to the paper submission website in order to maintain the consistency of author information among all publications of the conference.
144	If they are different, the publication chairs may resolve the difference without consulting with you; so it is in your own interest to double-check that the information is consistent.
145	
146	Start the body of the first page 7.5 cm from the top of the page.
147	**Even in the review version of the paper, you should maintain space for names and addresses so that they will fit in the final version.**
148	
149	### Abstract
150	
151	Type the abstract at the beginning of the first column.
152	Center the word **Abstract** in 12 point bold above the body of the abstract.
153	The width of the abstract should be smaller than the
154	normal column width by 0.6 cm on each side.
155	The abstract text should be 10 point roman, single-spaced.
156	
157	The abstract should be a concise summary of the general thesis and conclusions of the paper.
158	It should be no longer than 200 words.
159	
160	### Text
161	
162	Begin typing the main body of the text immediately after the abstract, continuing in two columns.
163	The text should be 11 point roman, single-spaced.
164	
165	Indent 0.4 cm when starting a new paragraph, except for the first paragraph in a section.
166	
167	### Sections
168	
169	Use numbered sections (Arabic numerals) to facilitate cross references.
170	Number subsections with the section number and the subsection number separated by a dot, in Arabic numerals, e.g.,
171	
172	> 1 Introduction
173	
174	or
175	
176	> 6.1 File Format
177	
178	### Footnotes
179	Put footnotes at the bottom of the page and use 9 point font.
180	They may be numbered or referred to by asterisks or other symbols.
181	Footnotes should be separated from the text by a line.
182	
183	### Figures and tables
184	
185	Place figures and tables in the paper near where they are first discussed, rather than at the end, if possible.
186	Wide figures/tables may run across both columns.
187	
188	To accommodate people who are color-blind (as well as those printing with black-and-white printers), grayscale readability is strongly encouraged.
189	Color is not forbidden, but authors should ensure that tables and figures do not rely solely on color to convey critical distinctions.
190	
191	**Captions:**
192	Provide a caption for every figure/table; number each one sequentially in the form:
193	
194	> Figure 1: Caption of the Figure.
195	
196	and
197	
198	> Table 1: Caption of the Table.
199	
200	Captions should be placed below figures/tables, in 10 point roman type.
201	Captions that are one line are centered.
202	Captions longer than one line are left-aligned.
203	
204	### Hyperlinks
205	
206	Within-document and external hyperlinks should be dark blue (hex #000099), not underlined or boxed.
207	
208	### Non-English Text
209	
210	Text in languages other than English should be accompanied by translations into English, and text in scripts other than Latin should \emph{also} be accompanied by transliterations into Latin script, since not all readers can recognize non-Latin characters easily.
211	
212	For example, παράδειγμα *paradeigma* ‘example’ is a Greek word, and this is a Greek sentence:
213	
214	> Αυτό είναι ένα παράδειγμα.  
215	> auto einai ena paradeigma.  
216	> ‘This is an example.’
217	
218	### Citations
219	
220	Citations within the text appear in parentheses (Gusfield, 1997), or, if the author's name appears in the text itself: Gusfield (1997).
221	Append lowercase letters to the year in cases of ambiguities.
222	Cite papers with two authors using both authors' names (Aho and Ullman, 1972), but cite papers with more than two authors by the first author's name and ``et al.'' (Chandra et al., 1981).
223	Collapse multiple citations into a single pair of parentheses (Gusfield, 1997; Aho and Ullman, 1972).
224	
225	Refrain from using full citations as sentence constituents.
226	Instead of
227	
228	> (Gusfield, 1997) showed that ...  
229	> In (Gusfield, 1997), ...''
230	
231	write
232	
233	> Gusfield (1997) showed that ...  
234	> In Gusfield (1997), ...
235	
236	Submissions should accurately reference prior and related work, including code and data.
237	If a piece of prior work appeared in multiple venues, the version that appeared in a refereed, archival venue should be referenced.
238	If multiple versions of a piece of prior work exist, the one used by the authors should be referenced.
239	
240	### Acknowledgments
241	
242	The acknowledgments should go immediately before the references.
243	Do not number the acknowledgments section.
244	Do not include this section in the review version.
245	
246	### References
247	
248	Gather the full set of references together under the unnumbered section heading **References**.
249	Place the References section before any Appendices.
250	Arrange the references alphabetically by first author, rather than by order of occurrence in the text.
251	
252	Provide as complete a citation as possible, using a consistent format, such as the [one for Computational Linguistics](http://cljournal.org/style_guide_refs.html) or the one in the [Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association](https://apastyle.apa.org/products/publication-manual-7th-edition).
253	Use full names for authors, not just initials.
254	Authors should not rely on automated citation indices to provide accurate references for prior and related work.
255	
256	As part of our work to make ACL materials more widely used and cited outside of our discipline, ACL has registered as a CrossRef member, as a registrant of Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), the standard for registering permanent URNs for referencing scholarly materials.
257	
258	All references are required to contain DOIs of all cited works when possible, or, as a second resort, links to ACL Anthology pages.
259	Appropriate records should be found for most materials in the current [ACL Anthology](https://aclweb.org/anthology/).
260	
261	Example article in a journal:
262	
263	> Rie Kubota Ando and Tong Zhang. 2005. [A framework for learning predictive structures from multiple tasks and unlabeled data](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v6/ando05a.html). *Journal of Machine Learning Research*, 6:1817–1853.
264	
265	Example paper in non-ACL proceedings, with DOI:
266	
267	> Galen Andrew and Jianfeng Gao. 2007. [Scalable training of L1-regularized log-linear models](https://doi.org/10.1145/1273496.1273501). In *Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on Machine Learning*, pages 33–40.
268	
269	Example ACL Anthology paper with DOI:
270	
271	> James Goodman, Andreas Vlachos, and Jason Naradowsky. 2016. [Noise reduction and targeted exploration in imitation learning for Abstract Meaning Representation parsing](http://dx.doi.org/10.18653/v1/P16-1001). In *Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)*, pages 1–45711, Berlin, Germany. Association for Computational Linguistics.
272	
273	Example ACL Anthology paper without DOI:
274	
275	> Benjamin Börschinger and Mark Johnson. 2011. [A particle filter algorithm for Bayesian word segmentation](https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/U11-1004/). In *Proceedings of the Australasian Language Technology Association Workshop 2011*, pages 10–44718, Canberra, Australia.
276	
277	Example arXiv paper:
278	
279	> Mohammad Sadegh Rasooli and Joel R. Tetreault. 2015. [Yara parser: A fast and accurate dependency parser](http://arxiv.org/abs/1503.06733). *Computing Research Repository*, arXiv:1503.06733. Version 2.
280	
281	## Appendices
282	
283	Appendices are material that can be read, and include lemmas, formulas, proofs, and tables that are not critical to the reading and understanding of the paper.
284	Letter them in sequence and provide an informative title:
285	
286	> Appendix A. Title of Appendix
287	
288	The appendices come after the references.
289	
290	Review versions of appendices must follow the same anonymity guidelines as the main paper.
291	
292	## Supplementary Material
293	
294	Submissions may include non-readable supplementary material used in the work and described in the paper.
295	Any accompanying software and/or data should include licenses and documentation of research review as appropriate.
296	Supplementary material may report preprocessing decisions, model parameters, and other details necessary for the replication of the experiments reported in the paper.
297	Seemingly small preprocessing decisions can sometimes make a large difference in performance, so it is crucial to record such decisions to precisely characterize state-of-the-art methods.
298	
299	Nonetheless, supplementary material should be supplementary (rather than central) to the paper.
300	**Submissions that misuse the supplementary material may be rejected without review.**
301	Supplementary material may include explanations or details of proofs or derivations that do not fit into the paper, lists of features or feature templates, sample inputs and outputs for a system, pseudo-code or source code, and data.
302	(Source code and data should be separate uploads, rather than part of the paper).
303	
304	The paper should not rely on the supplementary material: while the paper may refer to and cite the supplementary material and the supplementary material will be available to the reviewers, they will not be asked to review the supplementary material.
305	
306	Review versions of supplementary material must follow the same anonymity guidelines as the main paper.
307	
308	## Credits
309	
310	This document has been adapted from the instructions for earlier ACL and NAACL proceedings, including those for
311	ACL 2020 by Steven Bethard, Ryan Cotterell and Rui Yan,
312	ACL 2019 by Douwe Kiela and Ivan Ivan Vulić,
313	NAACL 2019 by Stephanie Lukin and Alla Roskovskaya,
314	ACL 2018 by Shay Cohen, Kevin Gimpel, and Wei Lu,
315	NAACL 2018 by Margaret Mitchell and Stephanie Lukin,
316	BibTeX suggestions for (NA)ACL 2017/2018 from Jason Eisner,
317	ACL 2017 by Dan Gildea and Min-Yen Kan,
318	NAACL 2017 by Margaret Mitchell,

322	ACL 2005 by Hwee Tou Ng and Kemal Oflazer,

324	and earlier ACL and EACL formats written by several people, including

# Instructions for *ACL Proceedings

The following instructions are for authors of papers submitted for review to ACL conferences (hereafter, "review version") or paper accepted for publication in its proceedings (hereafter, "final version").
All authors are required to adhere to these specifications.

## Style Files

*ACL provides style files for LaTeX and Microsoft Word that meet these requirements. They can be found at:

> https://acl-org.github.io/ACLPUB/

We strongly recommend the use of these style files, which have been appropriately tailored for the *ACL proceedings.

## Paper Length

The conference accepts submissions of long papers and short papers.
Review versions of long papers may have up to eight (8) pages of content plus unlimited pages for references.
Upon acceptance, final versions of long papers will be given one additional page -- up to nine (9) pages of content plus unlimited pages for acknowledgements and references -- so that reviewers' comments can be taken into account.
Review versions of short papers may have up to four (4) pages of content, plus unlimited pages for references.
Final versions of short papers may have up to five (5) pages, plus unlimited pages for acknowledgements and references.
For both long and short papers, all figures and tables that are part of the main text must fit within these page limits.

The conference encourages submission of appendices and supplementary material, which are not required to fit within these page limits. However, review versions of papers must be self-contained: it is optional for reviewers to look at appendices or supplementary material. Please see [Appendices](#Appendices) and [Supplementary](#Supplementary Material) for more information.

Review versions should not refer, for further detail, to documents, code or data resources that are not available to the reviewers.

Papers that do not conform to these requirements may be rejected without review.

Workshop chairs may have different rules for allowed length and whether appendices or supplementary materials are welcome.
As always, the respective call for papers is the authoritative source.

## Anonymity

As reviewing will be double-blind, review versions must not include any identifying information about the authors (such as names, affiliations, or URLs).
Self-references that reveal the author's identity, e.g.,

> We previously showed (Gusfield, 1997)...

must be avoided, and anonymous citations, e.g.,

> We previously showed (Anonymous, 1997)...

should also be avoided. Instead, use citations such as

> Gusfield (1997) previously showed...

Review versions must not include acknowledgements.

**Papers that do not conform to these requirements may be rejected without review.**

Any preliminary non-archival versions of submitted papers should be listed in the submission form but not in the review version of the paper.
Reviewers are generally aware that authors may present preliminary versions of their work in other venues, but will not be provided the list of previous presentations from the submission form.

Once a paper has been accepted to the conference, the final version should include the author's names and affiliations, and is allowed to use self-references.

## Multiple Submission

Papers that have been or will be submitted to other meetings or publications must indicate this at submission time in the START submission form, and must be withdrawn from the other venues if accepted by *ACL.
Authors of papers accepted for presentation at *ACL must notify the program chairs by the deadline for final versions ("camera-ready deadline") whether the paper will be presented.
We will not accept for publication or presentation any papers that overlap significantly in content or results with papers that will be (or have been) published elsewhere.

Authors submitting more than one paper to *ACL must ensure that submissions do not overlap significantly (>25%) with each other in content or results.

## Formatting Instructions

### File Format

Papers must be in Adobe Portable Document Format (PDF).
Please make sure that your PDF file embeds all necessary fonts (especially for tree diagrams, symbols, and Asian languages).
When you print or create the PDF file, there is usually an option in your printer setup to include none, all or just non-standard fonts.
Please make sure that you select the option of including *all* the fonts.
**Before sending it, test your PDF by printing it from a computer different from the one where it was created.**

Some word processors may generate very large PDF files, where each page is rendered as an image.
Such images may reproduce poorly.
In this case, try alternative ways to obtain the PDF.

All papers must use **A4 paper format** (21 cm x 29.7 cm).
Papers must not be submitted with any other paper size.

If you cannot meet the above requirements, please contact the publication chairs as soon as possible.

### Layout

All text except for page numbers must fit within the margins.

Review versions should have page numbers, centered in the bottom margin, but **pages should not be numbered in the final version.**

Manuscripts must be set in two columns.
Exceptions to the two-column format include the title, authors' names and complete addresses, which must be centered at the top of the first page, and any full-width figures or tables.

The exact dimensions for a page on A4 paper are:

* Left margin: 2.5 cm
* Right margin: 2.5 cm
* Top margin: 2.5 cm
* Bottom margin: 2.5 cm
* Column width: 7.7 cm
* Column height: 24.7 cm
* Gap between columns: 0.6 cm

In the review version, a ruler (line numbers in the left and right margins of the article) should be printed, so that reviewers may comment on particular lines in the paper.
The ruler should not change the appearance of any other content on the page.
The final version should not contain a ruler.

If Times Roman is unavailable, you may use **Times New Roman** or **Computer Modern Roman.**

| Type of Text          | Font Size | Style |
| --------------------- | --------- | ----- |

| author names          | 12 pt     | bold  |
| author affiliation    | 12 pt     |       |
| the word ``Abstract'' | 12 pt     | bold  |
| section titles        | 12 pt     | bold  |
| subsection titles     | 11 pt     | bold  |
| document text         | 11 pt     |       |
| captions              | 10 pt     |       |
| abstract text         | 10 pt     |       |
| bibliography          | 10 pt     |       |
| footnotes             | 9 pt      |       |

### Title and Authors

Center the title, author's name(s) and affiliation(s) across both columns.

Place the title centered at the top of the first page, in 15-point bold.
Long titles should be typed on two lines without a blank line intervening.
Put the title 2.5 cm from the top of the page.

normal column width by 0.6 cm on each side.

The abstract should be a concise summary of the general thesis and conclusions of the paper.

### Text

> 1 Introduction

or

### References

Place the References section before any Appendices.
Arrange the references alphabetically by first author, rather than by order of occurrence in the text.

Provide as complete a citation as possible, using a consistent format, such as the [one for Computational Linguistics](http://cljournal.org/style_guide_refs.html) or the one in the [Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association](https://apastyle.apa.org/products/publication-manual-7th-edition).
Use full names for authors, not just initials.
Authors should not rely on automated citation indices to provide accurate references for prior and related work.

As part of our work to make ACL materials more widely used and cited outside of our discipline, ACL has registered as a CrossRef member, as a registrant of Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs), the standard for registering permanent URNs for referencing scholarly materials.

All references are required to contain DOIs of all cited works when possible, or, as a second resort, links to ACL Anthology pages.
Appropriate records should be found for most materials in the current [ACL Anthology](https://aclweb.org/anthology/).

Example article in a journal:

> Rie Kubota Ando and Tong Zhang. 2005. [A framework for learning predictive structures from multiple tasks and unlabeled data](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v6/ando05a.html). *Journal of Machine Learning Research*, 6:1817–1853.

> James Goodman, Andreas Vlachos, and Jason Naradowsky. 2016. [Noise reduction and targeted exploration in imitation learning for Abstract Meaning Representation parsing](http://dx.doi.org/10.18653/v1/P16-1001). In *Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)*, pages 1–45711, Berlin, Germany. Association for Computational Linguistics.

Example ACL Anthology paper without DOI:

> Benjamin Börschinger and Mark Johnson. 2011. [A particle filter algorithm for Bayesian word segmentation](https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/U11-1004/). In *Proceedings of the Australasian Language Technology Association Workshop 2011*, pages 10–44718, Canberra, Australia.

Example arXiv paper:

> Mohammad Sadegh Rasooli and Joel R. Tetreault. 2015. [Yara parser: A fast and accurate dependency parser](http://arxiv.org/abs/1503.06733). *Computing Research Repository*, arXiv:1503.06733. Version 2.

## Appendices

Appendices are material that can be read, and include lemmas, formulas, proofs, and tables that are not critical to the reading and understanding of the paper.
Letter them in sequence and provide an informative title:

> Appendix A. Title of Appendix

The appendices come after the references.

Review versions of appendices must follow the same anonymity guidelines as the main paper.

## Supplementary Material

Submissions may include non-readable supplementary material used in the work and described in the paper.
Any accompanying software and/or data should include licenses and documentation of research review as appropriate.
Supplementary material may report preprocessing decisions, model parameters, and other details necessary for the replication of the experiments reported in the paper.
Seemingly small preprocessing decisions can sometimes make a large difference in performance, so it is crucial to record such decisions to precisely characterize state-of-the-art methods.

Nonetheless, supplementary material should be supplementary (rather than central) to the paper.
**Submissions that misuse the supplementary material may be rejected without review.**
Supplementary material may include explanations or details of proofs or derivations that do not fit into the paper, lists of features or feature templates, sample inputs and outputs for a system, pseudo-code or source code, and data.
(Source code and data should be separate uploads, rather than part of the paper).

The paper should not rely on the supplementary material: while the paper may refer to and cite the supplementary material and the supplementary material will be available to the reviewers, they will not be asked to review the supplementary material.

Review versions of supplementary material must follow the same anonymity guidelines as the main paper.

15	We identify four deficiencies in existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
16	(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
17	(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined.
18	(3)~No FDR correction guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
19	(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
20	
21	We discover a \emph{detection phase transition} in canary-based monitoring of iterative collapse.
22	Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across thirteen contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50, 0.55, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we show that causal detectability undergoes a steep onset at per-generation mixing ratio $\alpha_c{=}0.476$ at $T{=}10$ generations (sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$): permutation Granger causality (PermG) jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant metric pairs at $\alpha{\leq}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$.
23	A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
24	A multi-method consensus framework (MMCT) comparing five statistical methods reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
25	Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
26	Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.
27	
28	Our contributions are:
29	\begin{enumerate}
30	    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
31	    At $T{=}10$, PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), with a four-regime structure: \emph{blind}, \emph{onset}, \emph{synchronous dip}, and \emph{detection}.
32	    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null.
33	    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations confirms detection in 13 cases (87\%).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.

Yet a fundamental question remains unanswered: \emph{at what contamination level does causal detection of collapse become possible?}
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends depends on contamination regime and statistical method in ways that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.

We identify four deficiencies in existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined.
(3)~No FDR correction guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.

A signal-times-resolution ($S \times R$) framework explains this onset and the non-monotonic dose-response through competing signal strength and temporal resolution.
A multi-method consensus framework (MMCT) comparing five statistical methods reveals that method choice alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations spanning six families (345M--6.9B) confirms PermG detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 13 cases (87\%).
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}), not model collapse broadly.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Detection phase transition} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    At $T{=}10$, PermG jumps from 0/8 FDR-significant pairs through $\alpha{=}0.45$ to 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$, sigmoid $R^2{=}0.969$, $\Delta\alpha{\approx}0.02$), with a four-regime structure: \emph{blind}, \emph{onset}, \emph{synchronous dip}, and \emph{detection}.
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null.
    Cross-architecture validation across 15 model-seed combinations confirms detection in 13 cases (87\%).

    A power interpretation formalizes the onset as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}/\sigma)$, generating three testable predictions for $T{=}20$; sub-threshold PermG $p$-values at $\alpha{=}0.45$ ($p{=}0.059$--$0.091$) are consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

    \item \textbf{Multi-method diagnostic toolkit} (\S\ref{sec:method}).

186	\label{app:change_point}

188	We apply a max-split change-point test with bootstrap significance assessment ($n{=}5{,}000$, $p{<}0.05$) to each metric's generation-level time series ($T{=}11$).
189	
190	Under the null control ($\alpha{=}0.00$, 3~seeds), downstream diversity metrics (distinct-1, distinct-2, distinct-3) produce significant change-points at generation~2 in all seeds (9/9 tests). Individual change-point significance therefore cannot serve as standalone evidence for a canary-specific effect.

192	Although individual significance is unreliable as a discriminator, the temporal ordering of detected change-points reverses between null and treatment conditions. 258	\label{app:csmp}

260	We translate the Granger-precedence finding into a deployable monitoring protocol using CUSUM (cumulative sum) sequential testing, calibrated against the $\alpha{=}0.0$ null control.

315	\section{Background and Notation}
316	\label{app:background}
317	\label{sec:background}
318	
319	This section establishes the formal setup and notation used throughout the paper.
320	
321	\paragraph{Iterative training loop.}
322	Let $M_0$ denote a pretrained language model and $\mathcal{D}_\text{real}$ a fixed corpus of human-written text.
323	At each generation $t \geq 1$, the model $M_{t-1}$ generates a synthetic corpus $\mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)}$, and the next-generation model $M_t$ is fine-tuned on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data:
324	\begin{equation}
325	    \mathcal{D}_\text{train}^{(t)} = \alpha \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{synth}^{(t-1)} \;+\; (1{-}\alpha) \cdot \mathcal{D}_\text{real}, \quad \alpha \in [0, 1].
326	    \label{eq:mixing}
327	\end{equation}
328	At $\alpha{=}1.0$, this reduces to the full-replacement paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}.
329	
330	\paragraph{Metric families.}
331	\emph{Canary metrics}: token entropy ($H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ on held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
332	\emph{Downstream metrics}: distinct-$n$ ($n \in \{1, 2, 3\}$)~\cite{li2016diversity} and perplexity.
333	Each metric produces a time series of $T{+}1$ observations.
334	
335	\paragraph{Lead-lag testing.}
336	Given canary series $X$ and downstream series $Y$, the central question is whether changes in $X$ temporally precede changes in $Y$, requiring directionality and confounder control beyond simple correlation.
337	We employ five methods spanning permissive to conservative: naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, threshold onset detection, permutation Granger causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality~\cite{toda1995statistical}.

367	\section{Extended Discussion}
368	\label{app:extended_discussion}
369	
370	\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
371	All FPR and FNR calibration results are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M, WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$, and six contamination levels.
372	Cross-architecture validation across 15 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: PermG forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 13 of 15 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting.
373	
374	\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
375	The unidirectional forward causation observed on WikiText (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all conditions) does not hold universally.
376	On C4 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling; however, this is seed-dependent (s43: 1/8) and noted as preliminary.
377	The practical implication is that directional asymmetry should be verified per domain.
378	
379	\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
380	The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: token entropy is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ on held-out real data, while perplexity is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ on model-generated text.
381	First-differencing removes their shared downward trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy leads diversity by one generation, whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because both co-move synchronously.
382	
383	\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints.}
384	Our application of Granger-type methods faces constraints absent in econometrics: (i)~observation length ($T{=}5$--$20$ vs.\ $T{=}100$--$1000$); (ii)~non-stationarity by design rather than incidental; (iii)~small multiplicity for FDR correction (8--32 pairs per regime).
385	Transfer entropy (0/192 FDR-significant results) confirms that method sensitivity extends beyond the five-method panel.
386	
387	\paragraph{Prevention paradox.}
388	Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence.
389	Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs), while threshold onset fails entirely (0/8), reinforcing the multi-method rationale.
390	
391	\paragraph{Canary metric choice.}
392	SmolLM3-3B reveals that canary metric selection constitutes a sensitivity dimension beyond the five statistical methods: token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations (0/4 significant pairs), while ECE maintains monotonic growth (3/4 pairs).
393	No single canary metric is universally optimal.
394	
395	\paragraph{Future work.}
396	Extensions include multivariate VAR models for confounder testing, multi-seed replication across all six architecture families, longer training runs ($T{\geq}20$), online monitoring within training pipelines, and accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking}.
397	The sigmoid onset boundary ($\alpha_c{=}0.476$) invites connection to the critical mixture ratio scaling law of \citet{gu2024cmr} and the data-mixing phase transitions of \citet{gu2025datamixing}.
